name: Henry David Thoreau
role: American essayist, naturalist and abolitionist (1817-1862); author of Walden and Resistance to Civil Government
summary: Transcendentalist who lived two years at Walden Pond, urged simple living, and refused to pay a poll tax to a government that upheld slavery and made war on Mexico. He holds that conscience outranks law, that the best government governs least, and that honest men should break unjust laws and accept the penalty, while defending John Brown's armed action. He distrusts majorities, politicians and the "improved means to an unimproved end" of new machinery.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: He asks of unjust laws "shall we be content to obey them" and answers that when a law makes you the agent of injustice to another, "break the law."

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: "It is not desirable to cultivate a respect for the law, so much as for the right. The only obligation which I have a right to assume, is to do at any time what I think right."

consent-of-governed.rationale: He says there will be no free State until it recognizes "the individual as a higher and independent power, from which all its own power and authority are derived," and that he cannot recognize as his government one which is the slave's government too.

civil-disobedience-accept-penalty.rationale: He urges that just men go to prison rather than pay ("the true place for a just man is also a prison") and did so himself, paying no poll tax for six years and spending a night in jail without resisting.

state-harmful.rationale: He accepts the motto "that government is best which governs not at all" as the end point, but says "I ask for, not at once no government, but at once a better government," and separates himself from "no-government men." Scholars read him as demanding a better government, not anarchy.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: He says all men recognize "the right to refuse allegiance to and to resist the government, when its tyranny or its inefficiency are great and unendurable," though he speaks of tyranny in general rather than of constitutional breach.

simple-living.rationale: "Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity!" and "Simplify, simplify"; he lived two years in a self-built cabin on very little.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Walden argues that most luxuries and the endless getting of goods hinder rather than help a good life ("Simplify, simplify"); he would let affairs be "as two or three, and not a hundred or a thousand."

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: "No humane being, past the thoughtless age of boyhood, will wantonly murder any creature which holds its life by the same tenure that he does. The hare in its extremity cries like a child."

animal-use-humane.rationale: He finds animal food unclean and thinks "it is a part of the destiny of the human race, in its gradual improvement, to leave off eating animals," while noting his own practice has been different.

refuse-to-join-illegitimate-government.rationale: To a tax-gatherer or other public officer he answers: "If you really wish to do any thing, resign your office."

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: "If a man does not keep pace with his companions, perhaps it is because he hears a different drummer. Let him step to the music which he hears, however measured or far away."

equal-moral-worth.rationale: He pictures "a State at last which can afford to be just to all men," and in his abolitionist papers demands the freedom of slaves and the rights of Frederick Douglass.

person-over-state.rationale: The State must "recognize the individual as a higher and independent power" and "treat the individual with respect as a neighbor."

tech-solves-problems.rationale: "Our inventions are wont to be pretty toys, which distract our attention from serious things. They are but improved means to an unimproved end," like a telegraph from Maine to Texas with nothing to say.

gradual-change.rationale: He rejects waiting to persuade a majority first: men "should at once effectually withdraw their support... and not wait till they constitute a majority of one."

democracy-best.rationale: He asks whether "democracy, such as we know it" is "the last improvement possible in government" and holds that "any man more right than his neighbors constitutes a majority of one already."

direct-action.rationale: He says "Cast your whole vote, not a strip of paper merely, but your whole influence," pressing refusal and imprisonment over voting as the means of change.

separate-church-state.rationale: He declined to pay a tax to support a priest ("I did not see why the schoolmaster should be taxed to support the priest") and "signed off" from the church.

universal-morality.rationale: In the John Brown papers he says the North "went behind the human law" and "recognized eternal justice," placing a standard above statute.
